lead: An SRS is the written contract between the people who need a system and the people who build it. It states what the software must do, for whom, under what constraints, and how acceptance will be judged. It exists because memory fades, teams change and 'fast' means different things to a user and a tester. You use it before design, during testing and after release when a dispute starts. A good SRS is short enough to read on a phone and exact enough that two readers reach the same test.
prereq: You need the split between functional and non-functional requirements from 2.1 and the validation checklist from 2.4.

blocks.text: The SRS turns scattered notes into one controlled document. It answers four questions: what is in scope, who uses the system, what rules and limits apply, and what evidence proves the system is correct. It is not a sales brochure and not a design document.
A practical IEEE-style order is below. The order matters: a reader meets the problem before the numbered checks.

items: Overall Description: product view, user classes, operating environment, constraints.
Specific Requirements: numbered functional and non-functional statements, each testable.
External Interfaces: user, hardware, software and communication interfaces.
Performance and Security: response times, load, access control, privacy, audit.
Quality Attributes: reliability, usability, maintainability and other -ilities with measures.
Acceptance Criteria: the check that closes each requirement.

blocks.text: Only the Specific Requirements layer carries the weight. The other sections make those statements usable. If a section has no effect on a test, cut it.

Write one requirement per numbered line, using 'shall'. 'Shall' marks a binding requirement. 'Should' is a goal, and 'may' is an option. Number in a stable way: FR-01, FR-02 for functional; NFR-01, NFR-02 for non-functional. Never renumber after review; add FR-06 instead.

A requirement is verifiable when a tester can pass or fail it without asking the author. Replace vague words with a measure. 'The app shall be fast' fails. 'FR-01 The app shall show an alert within 30 s of an official outage message' passes: 30 s is a number and the clock start is named.

items: Correct: it matches a real need from a named stakeholder.
Complete: no missing input, output, condition or error case.
Consistent: no two lines demand opposite behaviour.
Ranked: priority is marked, so low-value lines can wait.
Verifiable: a test exists and the result is pass or fail.
Modifiable: changes stay local because numbering is stable.
Traceable: each line links back to a source and forward to a test.

blocks.text: Use tables for data: an outage record can list time, area, message and source. Use diagrams only as support; the words carry the requirement. Use cases, class models and data flow diagrams get their own chapters: 2.6, 2.7, 2.8.

Review the SRS with users, testers and builders in the same room. Read each line and ask: can we test this, and do we know the source? A line with no source is a wish. A line with no test is unfinished.

Keep design out. 'Use Firebase' is a design choice; 'cache the last 10 outages for offline viewing' is a requirement. Keep the project plan out too: dates, effort and staffing belong in the plan, not in the SRS. The SRS says what must be true, not who will do it or when.

Acceptance criteria turn each requirement into a check. For an alert requirement, the criterion is: send an official outage message, wait 30 s, confirm one alert with the correct area. A change to any requirement goes through the change process in 2.4; the SRS stays the single visible version. The baseline is frozen at review; later edits are numbered versions. A reviewer signs the version they checked.

figure.caption: The SRS sections run top to bottom, and the worked example's five numbered lines all sit in section 3. Notice FR-01: it names the clock start and the 30 s limit, so a tester can pass or fail it.

spec.title: Chennai power-cut alert app: scope to numbered requirements
spec.aria: A flow from section 1 Scope for 20,000 Chennai users, through section 2 Overall Description, into section 3 Specific Requirements, which branches into the five numbered lines FR-01, NFR-01, NFR-02, FR-02 and FR-03 with their values.

examples.question: Write the SRS scope and five numbered requirements for a Chennai power-cut alert app for 20,000 users. It must send an alert within 30 seconds of an official outage message; cache the last 10 outages for offline viewing; run on Android 9+ and iOS 14+; let a user pick two areas; log every alert with time and area.
steps: Scope: a mobile app for 20,000 Chennai residents. It receives official outage messages from the electricity board feed, shows area-specific alerts, works offline for the last 10 outages, and records every alert.
Use three SRS sections: 1 Scope, 2 Overall Description, 3 Specific Requirements. Put the five checks in section 3.
Write the functional alert line with the clock start and limit: FR-01 The app shall show an alert within 30 s of receiving an official outage message.
Write the cache and platform limits: NFR-01 The app shall cache the last 10 outage records for offline viewing. NFR-02 The app shall run on Android 9 or later and iOS 14 or later.
Write the user choice and audit lines: FR-02 The app shall let a user select exactly two areas. FR-03 The app shall log every alert with its time and area.
examples.answer: Scope covers a 20,000-user Chennai alert app; requirements are FR-01 (alert within 30 s), NFR-01 (cache 10 outages), NFR-02 (Android 9+ and iOS 14+), FR-02 (two areas), FR-03 (log time and area).

traps: Writing design inside the SRS: 'use Firebase' or 'use RecyclerView' describes how, not what. State the observable behaviour.
Project plan creep: milestones, effort and team names belong in the plan; the SRS records requirements and acceptance.
Vague words: 'fast', 'user-friendly', 'etc.', 'robust' cannot be tested. Replace with a number, a condition and a clock start.
Mixing priority with requirement: marking everything 'must' makes ranking useless; mark high/medium/low and keep one meaning per line.
Forgetting the clock start: 'within 30 s' is incomplete unless you say from receipt of official message to visible alert.

quiz.q: List the eight SRS quality characteristics.
quiz.a: Correct, unambiguous, complete, consistent, ranked, verifiable, modifiable and traceable.

quiz.q: Why is 'The app shall be user-friendly' a poor SRS requirement?
quiz.a: It has no measure, no test and no shared meaning. Two reviewers can disagree, so it cannot be passed or failed.

quiz.q: Rewrite 'The app shall be fast' as a verifiable alert requirement with 30 s.
quiz.a: FR-01 The app shall show an alert within 30 s of receiving an official outage message. The clock starts at receipt and ends at the visible alert.

quiz.q: A line says 'Use Firebase to cache 10 outages'. What is wrong and what should remain?
quiz.a: It states a design choice, not a requirement. Keep the observable need: the app shall cache the last 10 outage records for offline viewing.

quiz.q: For 20,000 users, 30 s, 10 outages, Android 9+, iOS 14+ and two areas, write five numbered requirements.
quiz.a: FR-01 alert within 30 s; NFR-01 cache last 10 outages; NFR-02 run on Android 9+ and iOS 14+; FR-02 select exactly two areas; FR-03 log every alert with time and area.

quiz.q: What is the difference between ranked and traceable?
quiz.a: Ranked marks priority so low-value lines can wait. Traceable links each line to a source and to a test.

quiz.q: FR-01 says Android 9+ and NFR-02 says Android 10+. Which characteristic fails?
quiz.a: Consistency fails. Two lines demand different minimum Android versions, so builders and testers cannot satisfy both.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, the SRS becomes a requirements baseline in a wiki or issue tracker, linked to tests and code. Regulated domains add trace matrices and signed review records. Agile teams often keep living requirements in backlogs, but the same need remains: one testable statement per need.
